passages.text: Scleroderma Clinical Trials Consortium (SCTC) outcome instruments for evaluation of systemic sclerosis
Abstract

The Scleroderma Clinical Trials Consortium (SCTC) is committed to advancing the understanding and treatment of systemic sclerosis (SSc). This review focuses on the development and validation of various outcome instruments by the SCTC, which are crucial for evaluating the effectiveness of interventions in clinical trials and observational studies. Key instruments discussed include the Assessment of Systemic Sclerosis-Associated RAynaud’s Phenomenon Questionnaire, the SCTC Radiologic Scoring System for calcinosis, the Mawdsley Questionnaire for calcinosis, the University of California Los Angeles SCTC Gastrointestinal Tract Instrument (GIT) 2.0, the SCTC Activity Index and the SCTC Damage Index. Additionally, the SCTC and World Scleroderma Foundation (WSF) Skin Scoring Certification is highlighted as an important resource for researchers. Each instrument’s purpose, description and validation process are examined, underscoring their pivotal role in advancing SSc research and improving patient outcomes.
Introduction

The Scleroderma Clinical Trials Consortium (SCTC), a global organisation representing researchers and clinicians with expertise in systemic sclerosis (SSc). The mission of the SCTC is to advance the understanding and treatment of SSc by promoting rigorous research. Because few well-designed and validated instruments exist to measure the most common outcomes in SSc clinical trials, a key focus of the SCTC is to develop new outcome measures that will be needed for this purpose. To support this mission, the SCTC has created multiple working groups, many of whom have developed these new outcome instruments. This overview examines the purpose, description and accessibility of each SCTC instrument, highlighting their pivotal role in advancing SSc research.
Measures of vascular disease
Raynaud phenomenon: Assessment of Systemic Sclerosis-Associated RAynaud’s Phenomenon (ASRAP)—John Pauling and Robyn Domsic

Raynaud’s phenomenon (RP) is consistently ranked highest in patient surveys exploring the frequency and impact of disease-related complications of SSc. Establishing treatment efficacy in clinical trials of SSc-RP has been challenging with no Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved medications for SSc-RP. The episodic nature of SSc-RP and its relationship with cold exposure has led to reliance on patient-reported outcome (PRO) instruments to capture SSc-RP severity. SSc-RP clinical trial endpoints have historically focused on a construct of Raynaud’s ‘attacks’, using diary-based methods to record the mean daily frequency and duration of SSc-RP attacks; typically alongside a daily assessment of the overall severity and impact of RP symptoms using a single-item scale such as the Raynaud’s Condition Score. Meta-analyses of previous clinical trials would suggest the benefit of existing vasodilator therapies for SSc-RP measured by diary-based instruments is modest at best. While this may be the case, concerns have been raised within the SSc community regarding traditional SSc-RP trial endpoints. Regulatory bodies seek the involvement of the target patient population in the design of PRO instruments when examining labelling claims in medical product development. There was limited target patient participation in the development of existing PRO instruments for SSc-RP, which may not fully capture the patient experience of SSc-RP. Against this backdrop, the SCTC Vascular Working Group was convened with the goal of appraising existing methods for assessing digital vascular complications of SSc, and where necessary, consider the need for the development and testing of novel outcome measures. A comprehensive scoping review and international qualitative research study were undertaken to explore the lived patient experience of SSc-RP. We identified a number of patient experiences that were not captured using diary-based approaches for assessing SSc-RP including pain, sensory symptoms (numbness, tingling and burning), impaired hand function, emotional distress and reduced social participation (figure 1). A conceptual framework was devised for a novel PRO instrument for capturing the severity and impact of SSc-RP that was fully grounded in the patient experience of SSc-RP. The provisional Assessment of Systemic sclerosis-associated RAynaud’s Phenomenon (ASRAP) Questionnaire item bank was devised with patient partner input and included response scales that conformed to internationally agreed standards. Formal linguistic testing of the items ensured they were concise, simply worded to avoid exceeding sixth grade reading level (based on the validated ‘simple measure of gobbledygook’ calculator), minimised ambiguity and/or cognitive difficulty and met accepted criteria for optimal translatability into non-English languages. Cognitive debriefing interviews using a scripted interview incorporating standard probes were undertaken within English-speaking target patient populations at both US and UK sites to evaluate respondent perceptions about the language, comprehensibility, ambiguity, relevance and content coverage of each of the items. An international multicentre validation study enrolled >400 patients with SSc from UK and US SSc centres over two consecutive winters. An advanced psychometric approach with expert input removed redundant and poorly fitting items (n=12), without eroding content validity. The retained 27-item long-form ASRAP questionnaire was calibrated and scored using the graded response model. A fixed 10-item short-form ASRAP (ASRAP-SF) was developed using computerised adaptive testing simulations. The ASRAP questionnaires are scored using item response theory calibrations on the T-score scale (with a mean of 50, SD of 10 and a scorable range between 20 and 80).

The relationship between ASRAP questionnaires and demographics, clinical phenotype and legacy instruments for assessing SSc-RP severity, disability and pain was assessed. There was good correlation between ASRAP (and ASRAP-SF) and both the RP Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) and Scleroderma Health Assessment Questionnaire RP VAS scores (rho range 0.66–0.73, p<0.001). However, correlation with SSc-RP attack frequency and duration was lower (rho range 0.26–0.50, p<0.001) (figure 2). There was good correlation with instruments for assessing disability, hand function, pain and global health (rho range 0.427–0.575, p<0.001). Significantly higher ASRAP scores were identified in smokers, patients with active digital ulceration (DU), history of DU and calcinosis (p<0.05 for all comparisons). Repeatability at 1-week among patients with stable SSc-RP symptoms was excellent (intraclass coefficients of 0.891 and 0.848, p<0.001). Patient-acceptable symptom state thresholds and a preliminary minimally important clinical difference threshold have been estimated. Ongoing work examining responsiveness to seasonal variation in weather and pharmacological intervention is underway. Work is also underway to translate ASRAP into French, Dutch, Spanish and Turkish languages.

ASRAP, Assessment of Systemic sclerosis-associated RAynaud’s Phenomenon; RP, Raynaud’s phenomenon; VAS, Visual Analogue Scale.

The ASRAP Questionnaire is a novel and valid PRO instrument for assessing the severity and impact of SSc-RP that has been developed with extensive SSc patient input, with items grounded in the lived experience of SSc-RP to ensure strong content validity. As such, the ASRAP Questionnaire captures the impact of SSc-RP on how patients ‘feel’ and ‘function’; important considerations for regulators when adjudicating on marketing authorisation of new treatments. It is hoped the ASRAP Questionnaire will support future clinical trial programmes for SSc-RP and it has already been applied in recent early phase clinical trials of SSc-RP. The ASRAP-SF could be readily applied in routine clinical practice and patient registries of SSc, where it may facilitate capture of much-needed practice-based evidence on the comparative efficacy of different interventions for SSc-RP. The ASRAP Questionnaire forms are available online (online supplemental material, https://doi.org/10.1093/rheumatology/kead371), scoring software and interface is being developed to allow SCTC member institutions to use the ASRAP questionnaires in clinical practice and investigator-led studies.
Calcinosis
SCTC Radiologic Scoring System for calcinosis—Lorinda Chung, Antonia Valenzuela and Murray Baron

Calcinosis cutis is the deposition of insoluble calcium in the skin and subcutaneous tissues. It is a common and potentially debilitating manifestation in patients with SSc, most frequently affecting the hands and particularly the fingers. Although significant progress has been made over the past several years in the development and validation of outcome measures for SSc clinical trials, until recently, there were no tools to measure calcinosis in a standardised fashion, limiting the evaluation of pharmacologic therapies for calcinosis.

The SCTC Calcinosis Working Group has developed a radiographic scoring system to assess the severity of hand calcinosis in patients with SSc. This system uses anteroposterior radiographs of both hands and evaluates calcinosis based on anatomic location, percentage of area coverage and density. To ensure comprehensive assessment, the hand is divided into 22 anatomical regions, with each region assigned a weight proportional to its relative surface area. This design allows the rater to focus on one region at a time to estimate the percentage of calcinosis coverage within that region. The density of calcinosis is categorised as low density=less dense than trabecular bone; medium=similar to trabecular bone; and high=similar to or more dense than bone cortex (figure 3). The scoring process is facilitated using a spreadsheet preloaded with all regional weights, eliminating the need for manual calculations.

Scleroderma Clinical Trials Consortium calcinosis scoring system. The left and right hands were divided into 22 anatomic regions, which were defined by the underlying osseous structures but included the bone and surrounding soft tissue (A). Investigators were instructed to estimate the percentage area covered with calcium to the nearest 1% for each anatomic region (B). Reprinted with permission from Chung et al aug;67: 425–430.

The validation study involved 12 investigators—8 rheumatologists, 1 dermatologist and 3 radiologists—who scored 12 hand radiographs in random order. The scoring system demonstrated high feasibility, with an average completion time of 4 min. It also showed excellent reliability, both within and between raters, with intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) of 0.93 (range: 0.89–0.97) for intrarater reliability and 0.89 (range: 0.86–0.92) for inter-rater reliability.

This was confirmed in a study involving 39 patients with SSc with calcinosis across six centres in the USA, Canada, Mexico and Australia. Baseline and 1-year hand radiographs were evaluated by a radiologist and a rheumatologist using the SCTC Radiologic Scoring System for calcinosis alongside a 5-point Likert scale (1=a lot better, 2=a little better, 3=no change, 4=a little worse, 5=a lot worse). The scoring system demonstrated high inter-rater reliability, with an ICC of 0.93. This study also evaluated the scoring system’s effectiveness in detecting changes over time. By optimising the Kappa coefficient of agreement between the grouped Likert scale (better/no change/worse) and the percentage change in calcinosis scores, progressive calcinosis was defined as a >25% increase from baseline at 1 year, stable calcinosis as a change between −25% and 25% and improvement as a >25% decrease. The system effectively captured these changes: after 1 year, 41% of patients showed progression, 46% remained stable and 13% improved. These findings were validated in an independent cohort of 19 patients with SSc, reinforcing the system’s reliability and its ability to detect changes over time: 37% of patients in this cohort exhibited progression within a year, while only a minority experienced improvement.

The SCTC radiologic scoring system was used in a prospective, open-label pilot study to assess the efficacy of oral treprostinil in preventing the progression of hand calcinosis in 12 patients with SSc with radiologically confirmed calcinosis. The SCTC radiographic scoring system was the primary outcome measure, allowing for a quantitative comparison of calcinosis burden in the treatment group after 1 year relative to baseline. Baseline SCTC radiographic scores ranged from 14 to 2327.5. Among the five patients who completed 12-month treatment, four had stable calcinosis, while one showed progression (median 1-year % change: 22.2%, range: 5.3–85.5%). There was a significant association between final Likert scores and changes in SCTC radiographic scores, particularly when categorised as worsened versus improved/stable (kappa=0.56, 95% CI 0.06 to 1; p=0.049).

The radiologic scoring system was also used in a single-centre case series involving eight patients with refractory SSc-related calcinosis treated with one or more cycles of off-label rituximab (1 g every 2 weeks). The study found that two patients (25%) showed a significant reduction in calcification size on X-ray. Notably, one patient’s total score decreased from 677.4 to 31.3 after 46 months of therapy, while another patient had a reduction in calcinosis in the fat pad of the left third fingertip, with SCTC scores decreasing from 2.8 to 1.0 with treatment.

In conclusion, the SCTC radiographic scoring system has proven to be feasible, reliable and sensitive to change for assessing calcinosis in patients with SSc with excellent inter-rater and intrarater reliability. Additionally, its initial applications in evaluating treatment efficacy, such as with rituximab and oral treprostinil, highlight its potential in guiding therapeutic decisions and monitoring disease progression. The radiologic scoring system for hand calcinosis in SSc is available on request.
Mawdsley Questionnaire—Lesley Saketkoo, Kim Fligelstone and Anne-Marie Russell

As a lived experience, SSc-calcinosis can be asymptomatic but commonly it is debilitating and associated with constant pain, even at rest with subsequent impairment of hand use during routine life activities. SSc-calcinosis can interfere with major life areas that are foundational to health-related quality of life (HRQoL). Despite high personal impact and the development of promising measures that characterise the extent of solid formations of SSc-calcinosis, there had been no studies into patient experiences of living with SSc-calcinosis in the period prior to the investigations that produced the Mawdsley Calcinosis Questionnaire (MCQ).

With collaborative support from Scleroderma & Raynaud UK, the Scleroderma Foundation and the Federation of European Scleroderma Associations, the MCQ for SSc was developed according to FDA Guidance. It is the first PRO measure for use in clinical practice and clinical trials to evaluate and monitor SSc-calcinosis that captures a patient’s symptomatic and functional experience.

The stewardship and scientific engagement by patient research partners with experience in peer leadership and SSc qualitative research were essential in facilitating a feasible, effective design. The global design sought to achieve diversity in representation of age, gender, race, disease duration, SSc phenotype and geographic, cultural and ethnic participation.

Patient-driven question development and field-testing propelled the development of the MSQ. Forty international participants living with SSc-calcinosis who were >18 years of age and satisfied the American College of Rheumatology/the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology classification criteria participated in one or more investigational stages. Rigorous qualitative investigations yielded 78 discrete items arising during interviews and focus groups which were heavily populated with surprising patient-provided insights into the natural history of calcinosis and self-management. Through iterative analysis by a trained team that included patient research partners, these insights (items) were organised under seven overarching themes creating an overall conceptual framework that housed 21 major concepts.

Four domains (quantity/frequency, pain/sensation, physical function, psychological impact) that captured all SSc-calcinosis concepts relating to any sphere of function or body structure or impact on quality of life were identified as ‘actionable’ within the patient experience of body structure, function or HRQoL (including work, family and social activities). They were extracted by iterative analyses and consolidated into 21 potential PRO concepts. These concepts were qualitatively field tested for confirmation of relevant concepts as well as patient guidance on optimal language and selection of response scales. Subsequent quantitative patient preference studies yielded the final 17 scalable question items and 4 items that elicit open-ended responses.

The scalable question items fell under the following domains: quantity/frequency of calcinosis (four items), pain/sensation (five items), physical function/functional impairment (four items) and psychological impact (six items). Content and face validity were established. Two additional question items were direct queries into RP and DUs and may be considered ‘stabilisation’ questions, potentially to be scored separately for comparative reference. Further, the Scleroderma Health Assessment Questionnaire (SHAQ) VAS scales for RP and DU can also serve this purpose.

The generalisability of the MCQ was evident in the extremely high agreements across variable selections in the multichoice field testing phase. The results of the multitiered international qualitative investigations in SSc-calcinosis yielded remarkable insights into natural history, daily experience and complications of SSc-calcinosis providing pivotal information for health management.

Initial test–retest of the MSQ demonstrated good internal validity and moderate reliability in 19 patients with SS-calcinosis. Longitudinal validation work is in progress. The MCQ though not yet fully validated, is currently being used in multicentre clinical studies. In rarer diseases, this approach will determine concurrent validity with a range of measures and finalise a scoring and weighting system. These data from a larger cohort will enable rigorous psychometric testing using factor analysis to determine fit to the model and potentially identify weaker items within each domain. Correlative studies with measures assessing RP, DU and with functional and HRQoL PROs, including the Cochin Hand Function Scale, SHAQ and SF-36 are planned. Further, the MCQ items have been tested in patients and also parents of patients in a different disease, dermatomyositis, demonstrating strong internal consistency, with Cronbach α of 0.91 for eight MCQ items in adults and 0.90 for parent raters, correlating with severity when compared with a VAS of ‘calcinosis severity’. Translation of the MCQ is planned for in several languages via standardised translation protocols. The MCQ is copyrighted. License for use can be obtained by contacting Lesley Ann Saketkoo.
Measures of gastrointestinal disease
University of California Los Angeles (UCLA) SCTC Gastrointestinal Tract Instrument (GIT) V.2.0—Dinesh Khanna and Tracy Frech

Gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms are frequent in SSc. Their assessment should address both the severity of involvement and the response to treatment. University of California Los Angeles (UCLA) SCTC Gastrointestinal Tract Instrument (GIT) V.2.0 is a 34-item instrument with seven scales that assesses the breadth and depth of GI involvement in SSc. It was developed using the FDA Draft Guidance on patient reported outcome measure. It captures presence and severity of symptoms using five scales—reflux, distention/bloating, constipation, diarrhoea and faecal soilage and impact of these symptoms on social and emotional well-being using an additional two scales. Each individual scale is psychometrically valid. The instrument also provides a total GIT Score, which captures the overall GI burden. It was developed in patients with SSc with GI involvement using focus groups and cognitive debriefing and validated in a cohort of patients with SSc-GI involvement. Each item asks about symptoms over past 7 days (based on patients’ input) on an ordinal scale (symptoms and impacts are captured as no days, 1–2 days, 3–4 days or 5–7 days, except for a single item each for constipation and diarrhoea, which is captured as yes and no) and each scale and total GIT Score is assessed from 0 (no GI symptoms and its impact on well-being) to 3, with a higher score associated with more GI symptoms and greater impact on well-being. The GIT V.2.0 meets the OMERACT (Outcome Measures in Rheumatology) criteria for truth, feasibility and discrimination. It takes 5–7 min to complete the questionnaire and has been included in multiple observational studies and clinical trials. It was originally developed in English and has been translated into 78 additional languages. It is available for observational studies and clinical trials at https://www.rws.com/industries/life-sciences/instruments/ucla-sctc-git-2-0/ or from uclasctcgit@rws.com.
Measures of disease activity
Scleroderma Clinical Trials Consortium Activity Index (SCTC-AI)—Laura Ross, Mandana Nikpour and Murray Baron

The accurate identification of periods of disease activity has been a cornerstone of treat-to-target strategies across the rheumatic diseases. Targeted application of treatments or the escalation of treatment throughout periods of heightened disease activity have resulted in a reduction in the accrual of organ damage and improved patient outcomes in many multisystem autoimmune diseases. ‘Low disease activity’ has itself become a treatment target and prolonged periods of low disease activity are associated with improved clinical outcomes for patients. Targeted recruitment of participants with high disease activity may improve the likelihood of positive clinical trial outcomes by enriching study populations with participants more likely to respond to therapies under investigation.

The SCTC convened an Activity Index Working Group with the aim of developing an SSc-specific multisystem disease activity index that could quantify disease activity across the spectrum of SSc. The goal was to develop an instrument that builds on the previously developed SSc disease activity instruments. These existing instruments have faced criticism of limitations of face and content validity.

Measurement of disease activity in SSc has been a long-appreciated challenge, with there being an often unclear clinical distinction between features of disease activity and irreversible damage, an imperfect understanding of underlying disease pathogenesis and an absence of biomarkers of overall disease and vasculopathic and fibrotic mechanisms.

The SCTC Activity Index (SCTC-AI) Working Group represented an international collaboration of SSc experts from North America, Europe, the UK and the Asia-Pacific. Central to the development of the SCTC-AI was the first step of defining the construct of disease activity. Using consensus methodology that included a two-round survey and face-to-face meeting, the SCTC-AI Working Group defined disease activity in SSc to be:

‘Aspects of disease, attributable to systemic sclerosis, that are potentially reversible, or can be arrested, with time and/or effective therapy. Disease activity may be associated with morbidity and uncontrolled activity may lead to organ dysfunction and mortality.’

Potential SCTC-AI items were then generated from literature review and expert opinion from working group members, with potential items reduced via three-round Delphi survey. At each step, working group members were asked to consider whether potential items were a measure of the agreed on definition of disease activity to ensure that each item included in the final SCTC-AI had face validity. Data-driven item reduction occurred using data from the Australian Scleroderma Cohort Study (ASCS) and testing of the relationship between each individual SCTC-AI item and two clinical outcomes: death and morbidity, as measured by Short Form 36 Physical Component Scores. Items with a significant relationship with both outcomes were assigned an integer weight, calculated by combining the coefficients from the Cox proportional hazards regression performed in the item reduction phase.

The final SCTC-AI is a weighted, 24-item index measuring disease activity across nine disease domains with a maximum possible score of 140 points. Initial preliminary analysis of SCTC-AI in the ASCS and an external validation cohort derived from the Canadian Scleroderma Research Group (CSRG) Cohort Study shows a graded relationship between SCTC-AI scores and poor outcomes such as death and SSc-associated damage. Future work is required to test the performance of the SCTC-AI in a randomised controlled trial setting to evaluate the discriminative validity of the index and its sensitivity to change over time.

The manuscript describing the development and initial validation of the SCTC-AI has recently been published. A SCTC-AI data collection form and glossary of terms is provided in online supplemental Index 1.
Measures of organ damage
The Scleroderma Clinical Trials Consortium Damage Index (SCTC-DI)—Mandana Nikpour and Murray Baron
The SCTC Damage Index (SCTC-DI) is the first and only instrument developed to date specifically to identify and quantify organ damage across all the main organ systems involved in SSc.

A working group of 22 international expert members of the SCTC, representing Australia, the Americas and Europe, was led by a steering committee of six members. A panel of seven non-rheumatologist expert advisors covering the disciplines of cardiology, respiratory medicine, gastroenterology and nephrology, together with three patient partners provided input on item generation as well as ensuring the final instrument had face and content validity.

As a first step, the concept of organ damage in SSc was defined, using a two-round survey of working group members, as ‘permanent and irreversible loss of anatomical structure or physiological function, caused by SSc and not secondary to its treatment or comorbidities’.

Items for potential inclusion in the SCTC-DI were generated by the members of the working group, through literature review and consultation with expert advisors and patient partners. These items were reduced by survey of all members of the SCTC as well as by assessing the relationship of remaining items with mortality and morbidity using prospectively collected data from the ASCS. The surrogate measure used for ‘morbidity’ was the physical component score of the SF-36 instrument which captures health related quality of life. The weighting of the items was based on the strength of their relationship with these endpoints.

The SCTC-DI is comprised of 23 items in six organ systems, namely musculoskeletal and skin, vascular, GI, respiratory, cardiovascular and renal. Individual item scores range from 1 to 5 and are additive, with a total possible score of 55 points (figure 4). The SCTC-DI Score can only increase over time as it captures aspects of disease that are presently deemed irreversible. In this regard, it has been shown to be responsive to change over time in prospective cohorts. The SCTC-DI has been shown to be predictive of mortality and morbidity in an external Canadian validation cohort (the CSRG). Furthermore, there is a graded relationship between the SCTC-DI Score and risk of mortality.

The envisaged applications of the SCTC-DI include use as an endpoint in observational studies and clinical trials, as well as enrichment of recruitment for clinical trials. Further work is required to test the properties of the SCTC-DI in diverse cohorts and with varying disease durations. Application of the SCTC-DI in a clinical trial setting will enable further assessment of its discriminant validity. A detailed description of the development and initial validation of the SCTC-DI is provided in the published manuscript.
SCTC and WSF Skin Scoring Certification—Christopher Denton and Dinesh Khanna

The modified Rodnan skin score (mRSS) assesses 17 sites with an integer score of 0–3 and a maximum score of 51. Assessment provides a quantitative measure of skin severity and has been widely used in clinical practice and as an endpoint in observational and interventional clinical trials. Previous studies have validated mRSS as an assessment tool based on the OMERACT criteria of validation. Thus, it has been shown to have face validity (makes sense), content validity (covers the range of skin involvement), sensitivity to change (analysis of trials show change over time), is feasible (easy to do with little equipment, requires little time) and has criterion validity (reflects gold standard biopsy findings). However, there are limitations in practicality of mRSS in clinical trials, especially the well-recognised interobserver and intraobserver variability in mRSS assessment. Previous studies have shown that assessors perform better with much reduced variability if provided with formal training. To provide a standard approach the SCTC and WSF published an article describing the best approach to standardise mRSS assessment and to train assessors for clinical trials. This has now been widely used with >400 assessors now trained. Successful candidates at mRSS training courses are provided with a certificate that can be used to confirm training as a skin assessor in other clinical trials, although level of expertise and ongoing competency will be taken into account in determining need for refresher training for future studies. The SCTC maintains a registry of trained investigators and this information can be provided to sponsors that plan to undertake clinical trials in SSc.
Current recommendations for training are summarised below:
Recommendations for assessing mRSS in clinical trials

Teaching phase: video demonstration (by an expert examining a patient with SSc demonstrating different aspects of skin scoring) followed by a live demonstration by an expert on two or more patients with SSc.
Each trainee is strongly encouraged to review the Journal of Scleroderma and Related Disorders article.

Evaluation phase: each trainee examines at least three patients with SSc. These patients should be different from the training patients and should preferably reflect the inclusion criteria for the proposed trial.
At least two teachers will first examine each patient and record their mRSS.
Trainees will be given the mRSS sheet and asked to examine each patient.
Due to the measurement variability in mRSS, we recommend the following criteria for certification (figure 5). Typically, three representative patients will be scored.
Criteria for modified Rodnan skin score certification for clinical trials.

The COVID-19 pandemic limited opportunity for in-person training but this is now being delivered globally and is helping to ensure that mRSS is being assessed adequately in clinical trials where it may be a primary or secondary endpoint or included as part of a composite such as the revised Composite Response Index in Systemic Score.

Although the natural history of mRSS can be variable and important autoantibody associated differences need to be taken into consideration, the mRSS remains a valuable part of SSc assessment in routine practice and in trials. The SCTC–WSF certification provides a template that can be applied in studies and is an example of how standardised training can improve performance of a measure in clinical trials.
Conclusion

The SCTC has made significant advances in developing and validating outcome instruments that comprehensively assess various aspects of SSc. These instruments, grounded in patient experiences and developed with extensive expert input, provide reliable and valid measures for clinical trials and observational studies. The ASRAP questionnaire, SCTC Radiologic Scoring System for calcinosis, MCQ, UCLA SCTC GIT V.2.0, SCTC-AI and SCTC-DI are valuable tools that enhance the ability to evaluate treatment efficacy and disease progression in SSc. Furthermore, SCTC has standardised the approach to mRSS assessment, with organised training courses for assessors, and a registry of certified investigators—all aimed at improving the quality and consistency of clinical trials in SSc. Finally, additional outcome measures are currently under development within the SCTC, including tools to optimising the assessment of digital ulcers and classification criteria for scleroderma renal crisis and scleroderma heart disease—the latter of which has already been finalised and submitted for publication. Together, these efforts are expected to facilitate better therapeutic decisions, improve patient care and support the development of new treatments for SSc. Ongoing and future studies will continue to refine these instruments and expand their utility in diverse patient populations with SSc and clinical settings.
